name: Prajnaparamita
role: Perfection of Wisdom, honoured as a goddess and as a body of sutras
summary: Prajnaparamita means "Perfection of Wisdom". It names a family of Mahayana sutras and a goddess who personifies that wisdom, called the Mother of all Buddhas.
about: Prajnaparamita has two meanings in Mahayana Buddhism. It names the Perfection of Wisdom sutras, about forty texts composed between roughly 100 BCE and 600 CE according to scholar Edward Conze, including the Heart and Diamond Sutras. It also names a goddess, Prajnaparamita Devi, who personifies that wisdom and whom texts call the Mother of all Buddhas, since wisdom gives birth to awakening. She is shown in India, Nepal, Tibet, Cambodia and Java, often holding a scripture on a lotus.
kidSummary: Prajnaparamita means "wisdom that goes beyond". In Buddhist art she is a gentle goddess holding a book on a lotus, and people call her the mother of all Buddhas because wisdom helps everyone wake up. She is also the name of famous wisdom books, like the Heart Sutra.

story.title: Wisdom as a mother
story.text: Mahayana texts say that every Buddha learned from perfect wisdom, so they call her the mother who gave birth to all of them.

story.title: A book on a lotus
story.text: Artists show her with a scripture resting on a lotus. The book stands for the wisdom teachings written in her name.

story.title: A monk goes looking
story.text: In 260 CE, the Chinese monk Zhu Zixing travelled to Khotan to find the Sanskrit text. Local opponents, who doubted that the text was true Buddhist teaching, tried to stop it leaving. Zhu Zixing stayed in Khotan, but he sent the manuscript on to Luoyang, where it was translated into Chinese.

story.title: Texts travel the Silk Road
story.text: Monks translated the wisdom sutras into Chinese, and the Diamond Sutra copy printed in 868 CE became the oldest dated printed book known.

story.title: Wisdom in many lands
story.text: Her statues appear in Nepal, Tibet, Cambodia and Java. One famous stone figure from Java now rests in Jakarta.

teaches: Wisdom is the root of awakening
Look closely at what is really true
Respect for wisdom and for women
emblems: Perfection of Wisdom text on a lotus

facts.text: Prajnaparamita means "Perfection of Wisdom". The word prajna is feminine in Sanskrit, which helps explain why she is personified as a goddess.
The goddess form is younger than the books. The sutras came first, and only around the 7th to 8th century CE did the Perfection of Wisdom itself become a named goddess in her own right.

The sutras are bold about their own importance. The Ashtasahasrika says Buddhas owe their existence to the Perfection of Wisdom, and claims that honouring her is better than honouring stupas or Buddha relics.
The Heart Sutra ends with a short mantra, "gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha". Translators render it roughly as "gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond, awakening, hail!"
The largest Perfection of Wisdom sutra runs to 100,000 lines. Others are 25,000, 18,000 and 8,000 lines long, plus short ones.

The pilgrim Faxian wrote in the 400s CE that Mahayanists worshipped Prajnaparamita, but scholars doubt whether he saw a statue or only the book. Her earliest surviving images are at the Ellora Caves, from the 7th century.

A legend says the philosopher Nagarjuna brought the Perfection of Wisdom sutras back from the land of the nagas, serpent-like beings who guarded them. Some tellers place that land in the Himalayas and others at the bottom of the sea.
In Tibetan Buddhism the goddess Tara is often treated as an emanation of Prajnaparamita, so the wisdom mother is seen as standing behind other female Buddhas too.
Xuanzang's translation project covered 600 scrolls and about five million Chinese characters, and he chose to translate the full text after a series of dreams.

A Diamond Sutra scroll printed on 11 May 868 CE is widely seen as the oldest dated printed book. It is about five metres long, was found in 1900 in the sealed library at Dunhuang's Mogao Caves, and now rests in the British Library.
The 868 CE Diamond Sutra scroll carries a note saying Wang Jie paid for it on behalf of his two parents and offered it for free distribution, which has been called an early public-domain dedication.
According to Jacob Kinnard, the Perfection of Wisdom sutras treat the physical book as comparable to the Buddha's body, something to honour like his relics, as well as a container of his teaching.
The Heart Sutra's short Chinese version has only 260 characters, and it is chanted daily in nearly all East Asian Buddhist schools.

The Diamond Sutra's Sanskrit title means roughly the Perfection of Wisdom that cuts like a thunderbolt. Vajra can mean diamond or thunderbolt, and the image is of wisdom slicing through illusion to reach what is real.
An early hymn to her by Rahulabhadra, in translation, says that honest people see "no more difference" between her and the Buddha than between the moon and the light of the moon.

A partial Kharoshthi manuscript of the 8,000-line Perfection of Wisdom, found in Gandhara, is a copy of a text that radiocarbon dating places in the 1st or early 2nd century CE. That makes it one of the oldest Mahayana manuscripts known.
The Heart Sutra's best-known line says that form is emptiness and emptiness is form. Teachers read it to mean that things do not exist on their own, because everything depends on other things.
At Kwa Baha in Lalitpur, Nepal, a lavish 13th-century manuscript of her sutra is worshipped all year. Devotees told researcher David Gellner that the goddess herself is present in the book.
A famous story in the Platform Sutra says that the future Chan teacher Huineng, then a woodcutter, heard someone recite the Diamond Sutra and was moved to become a monk.
Cambodian Khmer statues of her are often esoteric, sometimes with many arms (one has 22), and often appear in a triad with the Buddha and Avalokiteshvara.
The 8,000-line sutra tells followers to set the book on an altar and honour it with flowers, lamps and incense. That is why a manuscript, like the one at Kwa Baha, can be treated as a living goddess.

A statue of her was found near Singhasari in Java in 1818 or 1819. Tradition links her to Queen Ken Dedes. It went to the Netherlands in 1820, stayed in Leiden for over 158 years, and came home in January 1978.
Cunda, another wisdom goddess, is also called the mother of Buddhas. Her statues are often hard to tell apart from Prajnaparamita's, and a scholar thinks that confusion may have been on purpose.

The woman mahasiddha Laksminkara wrote in her Adhvayasiddhi that no one should look down on women of any social class, since they are Prajnaparamita in human form. Tantric Buddhism often treated all women this way.

In the Heart Sutra, Avalokiteshvara, not the Buddha, explains wisdom to Shariputra. Jan Nattier took this as a hint that the text began in China, but Harada Waso and others reject that, so its origin is still debated.

quiz.why: Prajna is wisdom and paramita is perfection.

quiz.q: What rests on the lotus beside her in many statues?
quiz.why: Her key attribute is a Perfection of Wisdom text.

quiz.q: Which sutra survives as the oldest dated printed book, from 868 CE?
quiz.why: A Diamond Sutra scroll found at Dunhuang carries the date 868 CE.

quiz.q: Where did the famous Prajnaparamita statue of Java spend 158 years before returning to Indonesia?
quiz.why: It was kept in Leiden, in the Netherlands, until it came home in 1978.
